guide.title: Obstetrics & Childbirth
guide.lead: Most births need little from you: a warm room, clean hands and patience. Know when birth is too close to move, handle the few true emergencies (cord, breech, stuck shoulders, bleeding, seizures), and remember you now have two patients.

sections.title: Deliver here or go?
sections.question: Crowning, an urge to push, or contractions 2 minutes apart or closer?
sections.yes: Birth is imminent: prepare to deliver on scene (or stop the ambulance). Call for a second crew for the newborn.
sections.no: Transport on her left side. Ask: how many weeks, how many babies, waters broken (and colour), bleeding, problems in this pregnancy.

steps.title: Set up
steps.text: Warm the room or ambulance (23–25 °C). Delivery kit, two towels, a hat, and a bag-mask with a newborn mask ready.

steps.title: Head
steps.text: A flat hand on the head prevents an explosive delivery. If the sac is still intact over the head, tear it.

steps.title: Neck
steps.text: Feel for a cord. Loose: slip it over the head. Too tight: clamp twice and cut between.

steps.title: Shoulders
steps.text: Guide the head gently down to free the top shoulder, then up for the bottom one. The body follows fast and is slippery.

steps.title: Baby
steps.text: Dry, skin-to-skin on the mother, cover, hat. Suction only if the airway is blocked (mouth before nose). Check breathing and tone.

steps.title: Cord
steps.text: Vigorous baby: wait at least 60 seconds before clamping. Clamp about 10 cm from the baby and again 5 cm further out; cut between.

steps.title: Placenta
steps.text: Usually within 30 minutes. Never pull the cord, and don't wait on scene for it. Bag it and bring it.

steps.title: After
steps.text: Fundal massage until the uterus is firm, let the baby breastfeed, count soaked pads, recheck vital signs often.

sections.title: APGAR (at 1 and 5 minutes)
notes: 7–10 is reassuring. Don't wait for the APGAR to start resuscitation: breathing, heart rate and tone decide that.

sections.title: Delivery emergencies
rows: Cord at the opening before the baby
Knee-chest position or hips raised. Gloved hand lifts the presenting part off the cord. Keep the cord warm and moist; don't push it back. Go.
Hands off until the body is out to the umbilicus, then support it. Head not out after 3 minutes: two fingers in a V either side of the nose to make an airway, and go.
Can't be delivered in the field: knee-chest position, go.
Head delivers, then pulls back (turtle sign)
McRoberts (her knees pulled to her chest) plus firm pressure just above the pubic bone. Never pull hard on the head.
Uterus still large after the first baby
Expect a second baby within minutes and more bleeding. Call for more help.
Vigorous baby: routine care. Floppy baby: start breaths within the first minute; no routine suction.

sections.title: Bleeding and blood pressure in pregnancy

groups.title: Bleeding after 20 weeks
items: Placenta previa: painless, bright red bleeding
Placental abruption: pain, hard tender uterus; bleeding may be hidden
Never do a vaginal exam. Left side, oxygen to target, IV, go

groups.title: Pre-eclampsia
items: BP 140/90 mmHg or more after 20 weeks, and up to 6 weeks after birth
Severe: 160/110 mmHg or more, headache, vision changes, upper abdominal pain, confusion
Eclampsia: a seizure. Left side, airway, oxygen, glucose check, quiet transport

steps.title: Recognise
steps.text: 1000 mL or more, or any bleeding with signs of shock. A soft, boggy uterus (atony) is the usual cause.

steps.title: Massage
steps.text: Firm fundal massage until the uterus is hard. Let the baby breastfeed.

doses.note: Within 3 hours of birth; a second 1 g after 30 minutes if still bleeding

steps.title: Shock
steps.text: Two IVs, keep her warm, small fluid boluses, rapid transport and pre-alert. Don't pack the vagina.

rows.note: Or 10 g IM (5 g in each buttock) if there is no IV
Magnesium toxicity: knee reflexes gone, respiratory rate below 12/min

quiz.q: 38 weeks, contractions 2 minutes apart, urge to push, head crowning. You should:
options: Apply fundal pressure to slow delivery
Tell her to cross her legs
quiz.explanation: Crowning means birth will happen before you reach hospital.

quiz.q: 34 weeks: severe headache, blurred vision, upper abdominal pain, BP 172/108. Most likely?
quiz.explanation: 160/110 mmHg or more with symptoms is severe. She can seize at any moment: left side, quiet, rapid transport.

quiz.q: Pink all over, heart rate 120, cries when stimulated, moving all limbs, crying strongly. APGAR?
quiz.explanation: 2 points in each of the five signs.

quiz.q: Thick green fluid; the baby is floppy, not breathing, heart rate 80. Priority?
options: Start PPV within the first minute; suction only if the airway is blocked
Intubate and suction the trachea before any breaths
Rub the back until the baby cries
quiz.explanation: Routine tracheal suction for meconium is no longer recommended. Ventilation is the priority.

quiz.q: You see the cord at the opening before the baby. Best action?
options: Knee-chest position, lift the presenting part off the cord with a gloved hand, go
quiz.explanation: Keep the cord warm and moist; keep your hand in place until hospital.

quiz.q: Breech: the body has delivered but the head hasn't after 3 minutes. Next?
options: Two fingers in a V either side of the baby's nose to make an airway, and go
quiz.explanation: Keep the airway open until the head delivers or you reach hospital.

quiz.q: The head delivers, then pulls back against the perineum. First manoeuvre?
options: McRoberts plus pressure just above the pubic bone
quiz.explanation: This is shoulder dystocia (the turtle sign).

quiz.q: Heavy bleeding after birth, uterus soft and boggy. First action?
options: Pull the cord to deliver the placenta
quiz.explanation: Atony is the most common cause. Massage until firm, breastfeed, oxytocin per protocol.

quiz.q: 32 weeks, painless bright red vaginal bleeding. Suspect:
options: Placental abruption with a hard uterus
quiz.explanation: Abruption is usually painful with a tender, hard uterus.

quiz.q: Why transport a pregnant patient over 20 weeks on her left side?
options: The uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when she lies flat
quiz.explanation: Supine hypotension. If she must be flat, push the uterus to her left by hand.

quiz.q: During magnesium for eclampsia, her knee reflexes disappear and her breathing slows. Antidote?
quiz.explanation: Stop the magnesium and support breathing.

flashcards.question: Supine hypotension
flashcards.answer: After 20 weeks the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when she lies flat, cutting venous return. Turn her onto her left side, or push the uterus to the left by hand.

flashcards.question: Stages of labour
flashcards.answer: 1st: the cervix opens fully. 2nd: the baby is born. 3rd: the placenta delivers. Some add a 4th: the first hours after birth.

flashcards.question: APGAR
flashcards.answer: Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration; 0–2 each, at 1 and 5 minutes. 7–10 is reassuring. Resuscitation is guided by breathing, heart rate and tone, not the APGAR.

flashcards.question: Suctioning a newborn
flashcards.answer: Only if the airway is blocked or the baby needs breaths. Mouth before nose, gently with a bulb; deep suction can slow the heart.

flashcards.question: Prolapsed cord
flashcards.answer: Knee-chest position or hips raised, gloved hand lifts the presenting part off the cord, keep the cord warm and moist, don't push it back, rapid transport.

flashcards.question: Postpartum hemorrhage
flashcards.answer: 1000 mL or more, or bleeding with shock. Usually atony: fundal massage, breastfeeding, oxytocin 10 IU IM, tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours, rapid transport.

flashcards.question: Signs the placenta is separating
flashcards.answer: A gush of blood, the cord lengthens, the uterus becomes firm and rises. Never pull on the cord.

flashcards.question: Nuchal cord
flashcards.answer: Slip it over the head. If too tight, clamp twice, cut between, unwind it and deliver the baby promptly.

flashcards.question: Shoulder dystocia
flashcards.answer: The head delivers then pulls back (turtle sign). McRoberts plus pressure just above the pubic bone; never pull hard on the head.

flashcards.question: Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
flashcards.answer: BP 140/90 mmHg or more after 20 weeks (and up to 6 weeks after birth). Severe: 160/110 mmHg or more with headache, vision changes or upper abdominal pain. Eclampsia: seizure – magnesium sulfate per protocol.

critical.scenario: 39 weeks, waters broke 4 hours ago, crowning. As the head delivers you feel the cord wrapped tightly twice around the neck; it won't slip over the head.
critical.question: What do you do?

options.t: Clamp the cord twice, cut between, unwind it and deliver the baby without delay

options.f: The baby can't breathe or deliver with a tight cord.
That tightens the cord and injures the baby.
The cord is strangling the baby now.

critical.explanation: Then dry, warm, skin-to-skin, check breathing and tone, and record the nuchal cord.
critical.kpi: Manages a tight nuchal cord during field delivery

critical.scenario: 10 minutes after a field birth, the placenta hasn't delivered. Bright red blood soaks the towels; the uterus is soft and boggy. HR 124, BP 96/62, pale and sweaty.
critical.question: Diagnosis and priorities?

options.t: Postpartum hemorrhage from atony: firm fundal massage, breastfeeding, oxytocin and tranexamic acid per protocol, IV, rapid transport with pre-alert
Normal bleeding: monitor and transport routinely
options.f: Shock signs make this an emergency.

options.t: Pull the cord to deliver the placenta

critical.explanation: Tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin are the four causes; tone is the most common.
critical.kpi: Recognizes postpartum hemorrhage and starts uterine massage and rapid transport

critical.scenario: 32 weeks, first pregnancy: severe headache, blurred vision, swollen for a week, BP 178/114, vomiting. As you move her she has a generalized seizure.
critical.question: What is this, and your priorities?

options.t: Eclampsia: left side, protect the airway, oxygen, check glucose, magnesium sulfate per protocol, rapid quiet transport

options.f: A seizure with severe hypertension is eclampsia.
Nothing by mouth during a seizure.

critical.explanation: Magnesium is the drug of choice for eclamptic seizures. Ask about fetal movements once she wakes.
critical.kpi: Recognizes eclampsia and protects mother and fetus
